subject: biology
subtopic: Fatty-acid β-oxidation: counting acetyl-CoA, FADH2 and NADH for an even-chain fatty acyl-CoA
learning_objective: Calculate the number of β-oxidation cycles and the yield of acetyl-CoA, FADH2 and NADH from complete β-oxidation of an even-chain fatty acyl-CoA.
question: Myristic acid is a saturated, unbranched fatty acid with 14 carbon atoms. When one molecule of myristoyl-CoA undergoes complete β-oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix, how many molecules of acetyl-CoA, FADH2 and NADH are generated by the β-oxidation reactions themselves (before any acetyl-CoA enters the Krebs cycle)?
explanation: Each β-oxidation cycle shortens the fatty acyl chain by two carbons, releasing one acetyl-CoA and generating one FADH2 (at the acyl-CoA dehydrogenase step) and one NADH (at the β-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase step). An n-carbon even fatty acid yields n/2 acetyl-CoA but only (n/2 − 1) cycles, because the final 4-carbon unit (butyryl-CoA) is split in a single cycle into two acetyl-CoA. For C14: acetyl-CoA = 7 and cycles = 6, so 6 FADH2 and 6 NADH are produced. (These reduced coenzymes, together with those made later in the Krebs cycle, drive oxidative phosphorylation, but the question asks only about the β-oxidation reactions.)

option_analysis.A: Wrong: assumes one FADH2 and one NADH per carbon–carbon bond broken (13) rather than per oxidation cycle; only the six cycles generate reduced coenzymes.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: uses n/2 = 7 cycles and so counts 7 FADH2 and 7 NADH. This over-counts by one cycle — the last cycle cleaves butyryl-CoA into two acetyl-CoA, giving only (n/2 − 1) = 6 cycles.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: sets the number of acetyl-CoA equal to the number of cycles (6). The final cycle liberates two acetyl-CoA at once, so 7 acetyl-CoA are formed, not 6.
option_analysis.D: Correct: 7 acetyl-CoA (n/2) are formed in 6 cycles, and each cycle yields exactly one FADH2 and one NADH, giving 6 FADH2 and 6 NADH.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: treats each of the 14 carbons as yielding one acetyl-CoA. Acetyl-CoA is a two-carbon unit, so 14 carbons give 7 acetyl-CoA, not 14.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Amino-acid transamination and the urea cycle: nitrogen sources of urea traced with 15N
learning_objective: Trace amino-group nitrogen from an amino acid through transamination and the urea cycle to determine which atoms of urea become isotopically labelled.
question: A liver is perfused with alanine whose α-amino nitrogen is labelled with 15N; alanine is the only labelled compound supplied and all other nitrogen and carbon sources are unlabelled. Taking into account the reactions that channel amino-group nitrogen into the urea cycle, which statement about the 15N label in the urea produced is correct?

choices.A: Neither nitrogen atom of urea is labelled, because transaminases transfer the carbon skeleton and leave the amino nitrogen on the original donor.
choices.B: Only the aspartate-derived nitrogen is labelled; the carbamoyl-phosphate nitrogen can be supplied only by ammonia released from other amino acids.
choices.C: Only one nitrogen atom is labelled, and the carbon atom of urea also becomes labelled because it derives from the deaminated carbon skeleton.
choices.D: Both nitrogen atoms of urea can be labelled, because the 15N passes into glutamate, which supplies free ammonia via glutamate dehydrogenase and aspartate via transamination with oxaloacetate.
choices.E: Only the nitrogen derived from carbamoyl phosphate (free ammonia) is labelled; the aspartate-derived nitrogen comes from a separate, unlabelled source.

explanation: Urea, H2N–CO–NH2, has two nitrogen atoms with distinct immediate donors: one enters as free NH4+ (via carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I), the other is donated by aspartate (at the argininosuccinate synthetase step). Both nitrogens ultimately funnel through glutamate, the central collector of amino groups. Labelled alanine transaminates with α-ketoglutarate (ALT) to give pyruvate + 15N-glutamate. That glutamate can either be oxidatively deaminated by glutamate dehydrogenase to release 15NH4+ (→ carbamoyl phosphate → first urea nitrogen), or transaminate with oxaloacetate (AST) to give 15N-aspartate (→ second urea nitrogen). Hence both urea nitrogens can carry the label. The carbon of urea comes from bicarbonate/CO2 and remains unlabelled.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: assumes transamination moves the carbon skeleton while leaving nitrogen behind. In fact the amino group (with its nitrogen) is transferred to the acceptor keto acid, so the label does enter glutamate and then the urea cycle.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: assumes carbamoyl-phosphate nitrogen can come only from other amino acids. The labelled glutamate is oxidatively deaminated by glutamate dehydrogenase to give 15NH4+, so that nitrogen is also labelled.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: the urea carbon comes from bicarbonate/CO2, not from the amino-acid carbon skeleton, so it stays unlabelled; moreover both nitrogens, not just one, can be labelled.
option_analysis.D: Correct: the label enters glutamate by transamination, and glutamate feeds both urea nitrogens — free NH4+ (glutamate dehydrogenase → carbamoyl phosphate) and aspartate (transamination with oxaloacetate) — so both nitrogen atoms can be 15N-labelled.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: recognises the free-ammonia route but assumes the aspartate nitrogen is unlabelled. Aspartate is generated by transamination of oxaloacetate with the labelled glutamate, so it too carries 15N.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Gluconeogenesis: identifying substrates that cannot yield net glucose (even- vs odd-chain fatty acids, glycerol, lactate, amino acids)
learning_objective: Distinguish glucogenic substrates from acetyl-CoA-yielding (non-glucogenic) substrates and explain why even-chain fatty acids provide no net glucose carbon.
question: A hepatocyte with full gluconeogenic capacity is supplied, in separate experiments, with each of the substances below as the sole carbon source. Which one CANNOT serve as a net source of carbon for newly synthesised glucose?
explanation: Gluconeogenesis needs substrates that can be converted to pyruvate, oxaloacetate, or a glycolytic intermediate. Glycerol → dihydroxyacetone phosphate; lactate → pyruvate (Cori cycle); alanine → pyruvate (glucose–alanine cycle); and odd-chain fatty acids yield propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA, an anaplerotic TCA intermediate that increases oxaloacetate and thus gives net glucose. Even-chain fatty acids such as palmitate are degraded solely to acetyl-CoA. Because pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible and the two acetyl-CoA carbons are released as 2 CO2 during one turn of the TCA cycle (with no net gain of oxaloacetate), acetyl-CoA cannot yield NET glucose. Palmitic acid is therefore the only listed substrate that cannot supply net glucose carbon.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: assumes amino acids cannot be glucogenic. Alanine is transaminated to pyruvate and is a classic glucogenic substrate (glucose–alanine cycle).
option_analysis.B: Wrong: reflects the misconception that anything derived from fat cannot make glucose. Glycerol released from triacylglycerol hydrolysis enters as dihydroxyacetone phosphate and is fully glucogenic.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: treats lactate as a metabolic dead-end. Via the Cori cycle, lactate is oxidised to pyruvate and is a major gluconeogenic substrate.
option_analysis.D: Correct: palmitate is oxidised only to acetyl-CoA; pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible and acetyl-CoA's two carbons leave as CO2 in the TCA cycle, so an even-chain fatty acid provides no net glucose carbon.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: over-generalises the 'fatty acids can't make glucose' rule. Odd-chain fatty acids yield propionyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA, an anaplerotic intermediate that does give net glucose.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Glycogen breakdown: glucose-1-phosphate from phosphorolysis versus free glucose from debranching (branch-point ratio)
learning_objective: Relate the frequency of α-1,6 branch points to the ratio of glucose 1-phosphate to free glucose released during complete glycogen degradation.
question: In a glycogen molecule, on average 1 in every 12 glucose residues is joined by an α-1,6 glycosidic bond (a branch point). During complete degradation, glycogen phosphorylase releases glucose 1-phosphate from α-1,4 linkages, whereas the debranching enzyme releases each α-1,6-linked residue as free glucose. What is the approximate ratio of glucose 1-phosphate to free glucose produced?
explanation: Glycogen phosphorylase performs phosphorolysis of α-1,4 bonds, releasing glucose 1-phosphate, but it stops four residues short of each α-1,6 branch point. The debranching enzyme then transfers three of those residues to a nearby chain end and hydrolyses the α-1,6-linked residue, releasing it as FREE glucose. Free glucose is therefore produced only at branch points. If 1 in 12 residues is a branch point, then per 12 residues 1 is released as free glucose and the remaining 11 as glucose 1-phosphate, giving a ratio of about 11 : 1. (Physiologically, roughly 8–10% of glycogen glucose is released as free glucose, consistent with this estimate.)

option_analysis.A: Wrong: an off-by-one error that counts all 12 residues as glucose 1-phosphate. The branch residue itself is released as free glucose, leaving 11 as glucose 1-phosphate.
option_analysis.B: Correct: with one free glucose (the branch residue) per 12 residues, the other 11 are released as glucose 1-phosphate, giving a ratio of 11 : 1.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: assumes free glucose and glucose 1-phosphate are produced in equal amounts. Only branch-point residues become free glucose, a small minority of the total.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: halves the count with no mechanistic basis. The branch frequency (1 in 12) fixes the ratio at 11 : 1, not 6 : 1.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: inverts the ratio, implying free glucose predominates. Glucose 1-phosphate from α-1,4 phosphorolysis is by far the major product.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Fed–fasted switch: PKA phosphorylation of PFK-2/FBPase-2 and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate control of glycolysis vs gluconeogenesis
learning_objective: Predict the effect on hepatic fructose 2,6-bisphosphate and the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis balance when PKA can no longer phosphorylate the bifunctional PFK-2/FBPase-2 enzyme during fasting.
question: In hepatocytes the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2 is normally phosphorylated by protein kinase A (PKA) in response to glucagon, which lowers the intracellular concentration of fructose 2,6-bisphosphate. Consider a mutant hepatocyte in which the PKA phosphorylation site of this bifunctional enzyme has been altered so that the enzyme can no longer be phosphorylated. During fasting (high glucagon), what is expected in the mutant hepatocyte compared with a normal one?

choices.A: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate stays high, keeping PFK-1 active and FBPase-1 inhibited, so gluconeogenesis fails to increase and hepatic glucose output during fasting is impaired.
choices.B: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate falls further, strongly activating gluconeogenesis and causing excessive hepatic glucose output and hyperglycaemia.
choices.C: There is no change, because fructose 2,6-bisphosphate regulates only the direction of the Krebs cycle, not glycolysis or gluconeogenesis.
choices.D: Glycogen breakdown is blocked, because fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is required to activate glycogen phosphorylase.
choices.E: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate stays high, which inhibits PFK-1 and activates FBPase-1, so gluconeogenesis is enhanced.

explanation: Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (F2,6BP) is the master signal of the fed state: it allosterically activates PFK-1 (glycolysis) and inhibits FBPase-1 (gluconeogenesis). Its level is set by the bifunctional enzyme PFK-2/FBPase-2. In fasting, glucagon raises cAMP, activating PKA, which phosphorylates this enzyme — switching off its PFK-2 (kinase) activity and switching on its FBPase-2 (phosphatase) activity, so F2,6BP falls, glycolysis is turned down and gluconeogenesis up. If the PKA site is removed, glucagon can no longer trigger phosphorylation, so the enzyme remains in its PFK-2-active mode, F2,6BP stays high, PFK-1 stays active and FBPase-1 stays inhibited. The liver therefore continues glycolysis and fails to increase gluconeogenesis during fasting, impairing hepatic glucose output and predisposing to fasting hypoglycaemia.

option_analysis.A: Correct: without the PKA site the bifunctional enzyme stays in its PFK-2 (kinase) mode, so F2,6BP remains high, PFK-1 stays active and FBPase-1 stays inhibited; gluconeogenesis fails to rise and fasting hepatic glucose output is impaired.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: this describes the normal phosphorylated (fasting) outcome. An enzyme that cannot be phosphorylated behaves as in the fed state, so F2,6BP rises rather than falls.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: misidentifies the target of F2,6BP. It regulates the glycolysis/gluconeogenesis branch point in the cytosol, not the Krebs cycle.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: confuses the regulatory systems. F2,6BP controls the PFK-1/FBPase-1 branch point, not glycogen phosphorylase, whose activation depends on phosphorylase kinase.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: reverses the allosteric effects of F2,6BP. It activates PFK-1 and inhibits FBPase-1, so high F2,6BP favours glycolysis, not gluconeogenesis.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: DNA double helix: total hydrogen bonds in a duplex from percentage base composition (Chargaff's rules and A–T/G–C bonding)
learning_objective: Combine Chargaff's equalities with the different hydrogen-bond counts of A–T and G–C pairs to calculate the total number of hydrogen bonds in a defined DNA duplex.
question: A linear double-stranded DNA molecule contains 1,200 base pairs. Chemical analysis shows that adenine accounts for 30% of the total number of nucleotides in the whole molecule. Assuming standard Watson–Crick base pairing throughout, how many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together?
explanation: There are 1,200 base pairs, i.e. 2,400 nucleotides in total. Adenine is 30% of 2,400 = 720; by Chargaff's rule %A = %T, so thymine is also 720 and A+T = 1,440. The remaining 960 nucleotides are split equally between G and C (%G = %C), giving G = C = 480. Each adenine defines one A–T base pair (720 pairs) and each guanine one G–C base pair (480 pairs). A–T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds and G–C pairs have 3. Total = 720 × 2 + 480 × 3 = 1,440 + 1,440 = 2,880. The key traps are reading 'adenine = 30% of nucleotides' as 30% of base pairs, and forgetting that G–C pairs contribute three hydrogen bonds while A–T pairs contribute two.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 720×3 + 480×2 = 3,120 swaps the hydrogen-bond counts, assigning 3 bonds to A–T and 2 to G–C; the correct assignment is 2 for A–T and 3 for G–C.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 1,200 × 2 = 2,400 treats every base pair as having exactly 2 hydrogen bonds, ignoring that G–C pairs are held by 3 hydrogen bonds.
option_analysis.C: Correct: A = 720 of 2,400 nucleotides, so there are 720 A–T pairs (2 H-bonds each) and 480 G–C pairs (3 H-bonds each): 720×2 + 480×3 = 2,880.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 1,200 × 3 = 3,600 assumes all base pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds, which is true only for G–C, not for A–T.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 3,240 comes from misreading 'adenine = 30% of nucleotides' as 30% of the base pairs (360 A–T pairs, 840 G–C pairs → 360×2 + 840×3). The 30% refers to all nucleotides, so A–T pairs = 720, not 360.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Chargaff's rules apply to the duplex, not to a single strand: whole-molecule base composition deduced from one strand
learning_objective: Distinguish the base composition of an individual DNA strand from that of the whole duplex, and compute whole-molecule percentages from single-strand data using complementarity.
question: In one of the two strands of a double-stranded DNA molecule, the base composition is measured as: adenine 32%, thymine 20%, guanine 18%, cytosine 30%. Assuming standard base pairing, what is the percentage of cytosine in the entire double-stranded molecule?
explanation: Chargaff's equalities (%A = %T and %G = %C) hold for a complete duplex, not for an individual strand — indeed here the single strand has %A ≠ %T and %G ≠ %C. To get the whole-molecule cytosine content, average the two strands. The complementary strand's cytosine equals the first strand's guanine (C pairs with G), so C(strand 2) = G(strand 1) = 18%. Whole-molecule %C = (C₁ + C₂)/2 = (30 + 18)/2 = 24%. As a check, whole-molecule %G = (G₁ + C₁)/2 = (18 + 30)/2 = 24% = %C, and %A = %T = (32 + 20)/2 = 26%, summing to 100%.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 15% halves only strand 1's cytosine (30/2), incorrectly assuming the complementary strand contributes no cytosine.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 30% simply reports the cytosine content of the single measured strand as if Chargaff's %C = %G applied strand-by-strand. Those equalities apply only to the whole duplex.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: 48% adds the two strands' cytosine (30% + 18%) without dividing by two; percentages must be averaged over both strands of the duplex.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 26% is the whole-molecule %A (= %T); it confuses the A–T value with the requested G–C (cytosine) value.
option_analysis.E: Correct: the complementary strand's C equals strand 1's G (18%), so whole-molecule %C = (30 + 18)/2 = 24%.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Histone acetylation: lysine charge neutralisation, chromatin decondensation and transcriptional activation (consequence of HDAC inhibition)
learning_objective: Reason from the electrostatics of histone–DNA interaction to predict how inhibiting histone deacetylase alters chromatin compaction and transcription.
question: A researcher treats cultured human cells with a potent, specific inhibitor of histone deacetylase (HDAC). Assuming the inhibitor acts as expected, which of the following best describes the most likely direct consequence for chromatin and gene expression, together with its underlying biophysical basis?

choices.A: Histone acetylation increases, but because acetylation strengthens the histone–DNA interaction, chromatin condenses and transcription decreases.
choices.B: Histone tails become more positively charged, chromatin condenses, and transcription decreases, because acetyl groups add positive charge to lysine residues.
choices.C: DNA becomes methylated at CpG islands, chromatin condenses, and transcription decreases, because inhibiting HDAC directly activates DNA methyltransferases.
choices.D: Nucleosomes are stripped from the DNA entirely, so every gene in the genome is transcribed at an equally high level.
choices.E: Histone acetylation increases, the electrostatic attraction between histones and DNA weakens, chromatin becomes more open, and transcription of affected genes increases.

explanation: Histone tails are rich in lysine and arginine, whose positive charges bind the negatively charged phosphate backbone of DNA, favouring compact, transcriptionally silent chromatin. Histone acetyltransferases (HATs) add acetyl groups to lysines, neutralising their positive charge and loosening histone–DNA contacts, which opens chromatin (euchromatin) and promotes transcription; HDACs reverse this, recondensing chromatin. Inhibiting HDAC therefore leaves histones hyperacetylated: charge is neutralised, DNA–histone attraction weakens, chromatin opens, and transcription of the affected genes rises. Acetylation removes (not adds) positive charge, HDAC inhibition is not a DNA-methylation pathway, and the effect is gene-selective rather than a genome-wide loss of nucleosomes.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: acetylation is correctly predicted to increase, but the claim that acetylation strengthens histone–DNA binding is the opposite of reality — charge neutralisation weakens the interaction.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: this reverses the charge logic. Acetylation neutralises the positive charge on lysine, so hyperacetylation makes tails less positive, not more; the outcome is decondensation and increased transcription.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: this conflates histone deacetylation with DNA methylation. HDAC removes acetyl groups from histones; it does not control DNA methyltransferases, and inhibiting it does not condense chromatin.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: this overgeneralises. Acetylation loosens nucleosome–DNA contacts and biases genes toward expression, but it neither removes all nucleosomes nor makes every gene fire equally; regulation remains gene-specific.
option_analysis.E: Correct: HDAC inhibition causes hyperacetylation, which neutralises lysine positive charge, weakens histone–DNA attraction, opens chromatin, and increases transcription of the affected genes.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: 5' splice-site (GU donor) mutation causing intron retention and premature translation termination
learning_objective: Predict how a mutation in an invariant 5' splice-site dinucleotide affects splicing and, in turn, the mature mRNA and the encoded protein.
question: A eukaryotic protein-coding gene contains 5 exons separated by 4 introns. A single base substitution changes the invariant GU dinucleotide at the 5' end of intron 2 to GG. Transcription, 5'-capping and polyadenylation all proceed normally. Which of the following best describes the most likely consequence for the mature mRNA and the encoded protein?

choices.A: The poly-A tail cannot be added, so the mRNA is retained in the nucleus and no protein is made.
choices.B: Intron 2 is removed together with exon 3, so the protein simply lacks the residues encoded by exon 3 but is otherwise normal.
choices.C: Because introns are non-coding, their removal is not essential; the mature mRNA and the protein are unaffected.
choices.D: Intron 2 is retained in the mature mRNA and translation is likely to terminate at a premature stop codon within that intron, producing a truncated protein.
choices.E: The 5' cap cannot be added, so the mRNA is degraded in the nucleus before it can be translated.

explanation: The GU dinucleotide at the 5' end of an intron is the invariant donor (5' splice) site recognised by the spliceosome (U1 snRNP). Changing it to GG abolishes recognition, so intron 2 is not excised and is retained in the mature mRNA. Introns are not maintained in a reading frame and characteristically contain in-frame stop codons; a ribosome translating into the retained intron therefore usually meets a premature stop, yielding a truncated (and typically non-functional) protein. Capping (5' end) and polyadenylation (3' end) are separate processing steps and are stated to occur normally, so they are not the defect. Loss of a 5' donor site leads to intron retention rather than clean removal of the neighbouring exon, and introns cannot simply be ignored because they must be spliced out to join the coding exons.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: polyadenylation is a separate 3'-end event, stated to occur normally; a 5' splice-site mutation does not prevent poly-A tail addition.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: this assumes a donor-site mutation neatly deletes the adjacent exon while keeping the protein 'otherwise normal'. Loss of the 5' splice site prevents intron excision (intron retention); it does not cleanly remove exon 3, and the outcome is not a normal protein.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: introns are non-coding, but they must be removed so the coding exons can be joined in frame. A failed splice leaves intronic sequence in the mRNA, disrupting the message and the protein.
option_analysis.D: Correct: destroying the invariant GU donor prevents excision of intron 2, so it is retained; ribosomes translating into the intron typically hit a premature stop codon, giving a truncated protein.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: 5'-capping is an independent processing event and the question states it proceeds normally. A splice-site mutation does not block cap addition.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Processed pseudogene: origin by reverse transcription of a spliced, polyadenylated mRNA and genomic integration (retrotransposition)
learning_objective: Integrate features of RNA processing and reverse transcription to infer that an intronless, poly-A-terminated, direct-repeat-flanked gene copy arose from a mature mRNA via reverse transcription.
question: While comparing genomic DNA sequences, a researcher identifies a second copy of a gene that, in its original location, contains several introns. The newly found copy has all of the following features: it contains no introns and its sequence is perfectly colinear with the mature mRNA of the original gene; it is flanked by short direct repeats; it ends in a stretch of about 30 adenine residues on the coding strand; it lies on a different chromosome from the original gene; and it is not transcribed. Which process most plausibly generated this second copy?

choices.A: Duplication of the original gene during DNA replication, followed by enzymatic excision of the introns directly from the DNA.
choices.B: Direct covalent insertion of the gene's mRNA molecule into the chromosomal DNA without any DNA intermediate.
choices.C: Tandem duplication of the original gene by unequal crossing over between misaligned chromatids during meiosis.
choices.D: Reverse transcription of the primary (pre-mRNA) transcript before splicing, followed by integration of the resulting DNA into the genome.
choices.E: Reverse transcription of the mature, spliced and polyadenylated mRNA into a cDNA, which subsequently integrated into the genome.

explanation: Every listed feature points to a processed pseudogene generated by retrotransposition. The absence of introns and exact colinearity with the mature mRNA show the template had already been spliced; the ~30-adenine tract corresponds to the mRNA's poly-A tail copied into DNA; the short flanking direct repeats are the target-site duplications created when the new DNA integrated; and the copy lies elsewhere in the genome and is non-transcribed (it lacks its own promoter). Producing a DNA copy from an RNA template requires reverse transcriptase, so the copy arose by reverse transcription of the mature mRNA into cDNA followed by insertion into the genome. DNA-level mechanisms (unequal crossing over, replication duplication) would copy the introns and place the duplicate adjacent to the original; reverse transcribing the pre-mRNA would retain the introns; and RNA cannot be inserted directly into DNA without a reverse-transcription step.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: introns are removed from RNA by the spliceosome, not excised from genomic DNA. There is no cellular mechanism that cleanly deletes introns from DNA, and this route would not generate a 3' poly-A tract or flanking direct repeats.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: RNA cannot be covalently ligated directly into chromosomal DNA. Generating a DNA copy from an RNA template necessarily requires reverse transcriptase, i.e. a DNA (cDNA) intermediate.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: unequal crossing over duplicates DNA and would therefore copy the introns as well, and it typically places the duplicate next to the original — not on a different chromosome, and with no poly-A tract or target-site repeats.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: if the pre-mRNA (before splicing) had been the template, the introns would still be present in the copy. The observed complete absence of introns shows the template was the already-spliced mature mRNA.
option_analysis.E: Correct: the intronless, mRNA-colinear sequence with a 3' poly-A tract and flanking direct repeats is a processed pseudogene, made by reverse transcribing the fully processed mRNA into cDNA that then integrated into the genome.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Signal amplification: multiplicative gain through a GPCR-cAMP-PKA enzyme cascade with a non-catalytic binding step
learning_objective: Quantify the amplification produced by a hormone-triggered enzyme cascade, correctly distinguishing catalytic (amplifying) steps from a stoichiometric binding step that does not amplify.
explanation: Follow the cascade one step at a time, amplifying only at catalytic steps. One receptor activates 50 Gs, each activating one adenylyl cyclase, giving 50 active adenylyl cyclase molecules. Each makes 200 cyclic AMP, so 50 x 200 = 10 000 cyclic AMP. The activation of PKA is a stoichiometric BINDING step, not a catalytic one: 4 cyclic AMP are consumed per PKA, so 10 000 / 4 = 2 500 active PKA. Each active PKA is again catalytic, phosphorylating 100 phosphorylase kinase molecules: 2 500 x 100 = 250 000. The key trap is treating the 4:1 cyclic-AMP-to-PKA binding ratio as though it amplifies.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: 1 000 000 comes from treating the cyclic-AMP-to-PKA step as 1:1 (50 x 200 x 100), i.e. wrongly assuming every cyclic AMP activates its own PKA and ignoring that 4 are needed per PKA.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 10 000 is the number of cyclic AMP molecules; the candidate stopped at the second messenger and ignored the two downstream steps (PKA activation and phosphorylase kinase phosphorylation).
option_analysis.C: Wrong: 2 500 is the number of active PKA molecules; the candidate forgot the final catalytic step in which each PKA phosphorylates 100 phosphorylase kinase molecules.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 500 000 comes from dividing by 2 rather than 4 at the binding step (assuming 2 cyclic AMP per PKA), a common misremembering of the activation stoichiometry.
option_analysis.E: Correct: 50 Gs -> 50 adenylyl cyclase -> 50 x 200 = 10 000 cyclic AMP -> 10 000/4 = 2 500 PKA -> 2 500 x 100 = 250 000 phosphorylase kinase.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Gq-phospholipase C-IP3 pathway: calcium ions as a second messenger released from the endoplasmic reticulum
learning_objective: Interpret pharmacological and ionic-environment evidence to identify the Gq/phospholipase C/IP3 pathway and recognise that the resulting Ca2+ signal originates from intracellular stores.

choices.A: Diacylglycerol produced by phospholipase C diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and directly opens its Ca2+ release channels.
choices.B: The receptor activates Gq and phospholipase C, generating IP3, which opens channels in the endoplasmic reticulum and releases Ca2+ from intracellular stores.
choices.C: Membrane depolarisation opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, allowing Ca2+ to flow in from the extracellular fluid.
choices.D: The hormone diffuses through the plasma membrane and binds an intracellular receptor that opens Ca2+ channels in the endoplasmic reticulum.
choices.E: The receptor activates Gs and adenylyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP, which opens Ca2+ channels in the plasma membrane.

explanation: The three clues pin down the pathway. Because the Ca2+ rise persists in Ca2+-free medium, the Ca2+ must come from an INTERNAL store (the endoplasmic reticulum), not from outside. Because it is blocked by a phospholipase C inhibitor but not an adenylyl cyclase inhibitor, the pathway runs through Gq -> phospholipase C, not Gs -> cyclic AMP. Phospholipase C cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol; the water-soluble IP3 diffuses to the endoplasmic reticulum and opens IP3-gated Ca2+ channels, releasing stored Ca2+. Option B captures exactly this.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: it is IP3, not diacylglycerol, that opens the endoplasmic-reticulum Ca2+ channels (diacylglycerol activates protein kinase C at the membrane); this swaps the roles of the two phospholipase C products.
option_analysis.B: Correct: Gq -> phospholipase C -> IP3 releases Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum, consistent with persistence in Ca2+-free medium, block by phospholipase C inhibitor, and insensitivity to adenylyl cyclase inhibition.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: voltage-gated influx would require extracellular Ca2+ (contradicted by the Ca2+-free result) and would not be blocked by a phospholipase C inhibitor; reflects defaulting to the excitable-cell depolarisation model.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: this describes a steroid-type intracellular-receptor mechanism, which would not depend on a cell-surface GPCR or on phospholipase C activity; reflects confusing peptide/GPCR signalling with lipophilic-hormone action.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: a Gs/adenylyl cyclase/cyclic AMP mechanism would be blocked by the adenylyl cyclase inhibitor (it is not), and reliance on plasma-membrane influx contradicts the Ca2+-free-medium result; reflects conflating the cyclic AMP pathway with Ca2+ signalling.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Steroid vs peptide hormone action: intracellular receptor and gene transcription versus membrane receptor and second messenger, distinguished by sensitivity to a transcription inhibitor
learning_objective: Use response latency and sensitivity to a transcription inhibitor to distinguish the intracellular-receptor/gene-regulation mechanism of steroid hormones from the membrane-receptor/second-messenger mechanism of peptide hormones.
question: Two hormones act on the same target cell. Hormone P produces a measurable response within seconds, and this response is unaffected by a drug that blocks all new mRNA synthesis. Hormone Q produces a response only after several hours, and this response is completely prevented by the same drug. Which conclusion is best supported by these findings?

choices.A: P is a steroid hormone that crosses the plasma membrane, because its lipid solubility is what allows such a rapid response.
choices.B: Q is a steroid hormone acting through an intracellular receptor that regulates gene transcription, whereas P acts through a membrane receptor and second messengers on proteins that already exist.
choices.C: Both P and Q must enter the cytoplasm and bind intracellular receptors in order to exert their effects.
choices.D: The drug blocks P's response because peptide hormones ultimately exert all of their effects by switching on new genes.
choices.E: Q acts by binding a cell-surface receptor and generating a second messenger such as cyclic AMP.

explanation: The distinguishing feature is dependence on new mRNA synthesis. Hormone Q is slow and is abolished when transcription is blocked, which is the signature of a steroid hormone: it diffuses through the membrane, binds an intracellular receptor, and the hormone-receptor complex alters gene transcription, so the effect requires making new mRNA and protein and takes hours. Hormone P is fast and transcription-independent, the signature of a peptide hormone acting via a surface receptor and a second messenger that modifies pre-existing enzymes/proteins (e.g. by phosphorylation). Option D states both correctly.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: it labels the fast hormone as the steroid; steroids are in fact the SLOW hormones because their action requires gene transcription, not because lipid solubility gives speed. This is the classic 'lipid-soluble means fast' misconception.
option_analysis.B: Correct: transcription-dependent slow response = steroid via intracellular receptor and gene regulation (Q); transcription-independent rapid response = peptide via membrane receptor and second messengers acting on existing proteins (P).
option_analysis.C: Wrong: only the steroid (Q) enters the cell; the peptide (P) acts at the surface, as shown by its transcription-independent rapid response. Reflects the belief that all hormones use intracellular receptors.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: P's response is explicitly unaffected by the transcription blocker, so it cannot depend on new gene expression; reflects the misconception that peptide hormones act mainly by inducing transcription.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: Q is the transcription-dependent, slow-acting hormone (a steroid), so it does not work through a surface receptor and cyclic AMP; this mis-assigns the second-messenger mechanism to the steroid.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Receptor tyrosine kinase: ligand-induced dimerisation and trans-autophosphorylation, and the dominant-negative effect of a kinase-dead mutant
learning_objective: Combine the trans-autophosphorylation mechanism of receptor tyrosine kinases with simple combinatorial probability to predict the dominant-negative effect of a kinase-dead receptor co-expressed with wild-type receptor.
question:
A receptor tyrosine kinase is activated when a ligand causes two receptor molecules to form a dimer; the two kinase domains in a dimer then phosphorylate each other (trans-autophosphorylation), and a dimer can transmit a downstream signal only if BOTH of its partners have functional kinase activity.

A cell is engineered to express equal numbers of two forms of this receptor: the normal (wild-type) form and a 'kinase-dead' mutant that binds ligand and dimerises normally but has no catalytic activity. The two forms dimerise with each other at random. Compared with a control cell that expresses the same total number of receptors, all wild-type, the level of downstream signalling in the engineered cell is expected to be approximately:
explanation: Because the two forms are present in equal amounts and pair at random, each position in a dimer is wild-type (W) or dead (D) with probability 1/2. The four equally likely dimers are WW, WD, DW, DD, each 1/4. Only a dimer in which both partners are catalytically active can signal, i.e. only WW = 1/4 = 25%. Every dimer containing at least one dead subunit cannot complete trans-autophosphorylation, so the mutant 'poisons' the heterodimers. This is why a kinase-dead receptor is dominant-negative: it drops signalling to about a quarter of normal, far more than the 50% one might naively expect from losing half the receptors.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: assumes the mutant is simply a passive loss-of-function (recessive) so the remaining wild-type works normally; it ignores that mutant subunits inactivate the heterodimers they join.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: 0% over-applies the dominant-negative idea; wild-type/wild-type homodimers (1/4 of all dimers) still form and signal, so activity is reduced but not abolished.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: 50% treats the receptors individually ('half are mutant, so half the signal') and ignores that signalling requires pairs of active subunits, i.e. it neglects the dimerisation combinatorics.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 75% is the fraction of dimers containing at least one wild-type subunit (WW+WD+DW); it incorrectly assumes any dimer with one good partner can signal, whereas both partners must be active.
option_analysis.E: Correct: only WW dimers (1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4) are fully active, giving about 25% of control signalling and demonstrating the dominant-negative effect.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Apoptosis: the intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway, cytochrome c/apoptosome/caspase activation and Bcl-2 regulation, contrasted with the extrinsic pathway and with necrosis
learning_objective: Interpret experimental evidence to order the events of the intrinsic apoptotic pathway, identify Bcl-2 as an upstream anti-apoptotic regulator, and distinguish apoptosis from the extrinsic pathway and from necrosis.
question: In cells triggered to undergo apoptosis by severe, irreparable DNA damage, cytochrome c is detected in the cytosol before the executioner caspase (caspase-3) becomes active. Over-expression of the protein Bcl-2 prevents the appearance of cytosolic cytochrome c and blocks cell death. Which interpretation of these observations is correct?

choices.A: Bcl-2 is a pro-apoptotic protein that forms pores in the mitochondrial membrane to release cytochrome c into the cytosol.
choices.B: The cells swell and burst, releasing cytochrome c to provoke inflammation, as is characteristic of apoptosis.
choices.C: Activation of caspase-3 causes cytochrome c to be released from the mitochondria, which then inflicts the DNA damage that starts the process.
choices.D: This is the extrinsic pathway, in which a death ligand binds a surface receptor and activates caspase-8 independently of the mitochondria.
choices.E: Cytochrome c released from the mitochondria promotes assembly of a complex (the apoptosome) that activates an initiator caspase upstream of caspase-3; Bcl-2 acts earlier still, by preventing cytochrome c release.

explanation: DNA damage triggers the INTRINSIC (mitochondrial) apoptotic pathway. Pro-apoptotic proteins permeabilise the mitochondrial outer membrane, releasing cytochrome c into the cytosol; cytochrome c binds Apaf-1 to form the apoptosome, which activates the initiator caspase (caspase-9), which in turn activates the executioner caspase-3. The observed order (cytochrome c before caspase-3) fits this cascade. Bcl-2 is ANTI-apoptotic and acts upstream by preventing cytochrome c release, which is exactly why over-expressing it blocks both cytosolic cytochrome c and death. Option A states both the sequence and Bcl-2's role correctly.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: Bcl-2 is ANTI-apoptotic and preserves mitochondrial integrity; the pore-forming, cytochrome-c-releasing role belongs to pro-apoptotic proteins such as Bax/Bak. This confuses Bcl-2 with its antagonists.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: swelling, bursting and inflammation describe NECROSIS; apoptosis is a controlled process with cell shrinkage and no inflammatory release, and cytochrome c acts as an intracellular signal rather than an inflammatory mediator.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: this reverses cause and effect; cytochrome c release is upstream of caspase-3, not caused by it, and the DNA damage is the initiating stimulus, not a consequence of caspase activity.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: a DNA-damage trigger with cytochrome c release and Bcl-2 sensitivity defines the intrinsic pathway; the extrinsic (death-receptor/caspase-8) pathway is mitochondrion-independent, so the label is incorrect.
option_analysis.E: Correct: cytochrome c -> apoptosome -> initiator caspase (caspase-9) -> executioner caspase-3 is the intrinsic pathway order, and Bcl-2 blocks apoptosis upstream by preventing cytochrome c release.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Skeletal-muscle contraction: sliding-filament theory and sarcomere band changes
learning_objective: Apply the sliding-filament model quantitatively to predict which sarcomere bands change and by how much during contraction, recognising that filament lengths are invariant.
question: A relaxed skeletal-muscle sarcomere is 2.6 μm long. Its thick filaments are 1.6 μm long (defining the A band) and each thin filament is 1.0 μm long, extending inward from its Z line. The muscle is stimulated and the sarcomere shortens to 2.0 μm. Assuming the filaments themselves do not change length, what are the lengths of the A band and the H zone in the contracted sarcomere?

choices.A: A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0.8 μm
choices.B: A band 1.0 μm; H zone 0 μm
choices.C: A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0 μm
choices.D: A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0.3 μm
choices.E: A band 1.6 μm; H zone 0.6 μm

explanation: In the sliding-filament model the filaments do not shorten; the thin filaments slide over the stationary thick filaments. The A band is simply the length of the thick filament, so it remains 1.6 μm at every sarcomere length. The H zone is the central part of the thick filament that no thin filament overlaps. Measuring from the sarcomere centre (M line), each thick filament reaches ±0.8 μm and each thin-filament tip lies at (L/2 − 1.0) μm from the centre, so the H zone width = 2 × (L/2 − 1.0) = L − 2.0. At the relaxed length L = 2.6 μm the H zone is 0.6 μm; at L = 2.0 μm the H zone = 2.0 − 2.0 = 0 μm — the two sets of thin-filament tips just meet at the M line. Hence A band 1.6 μm (unchanged) and H zone 0 μm.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: makes the H zone widen to 0.8 μm. During contraction the H zone narrows (and disappears), never widens. Misconception: reversing the direction of filament sliding, i.e. confusing contraction with stretch/relaxation.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: the A band equals the thick-filament length and cannot change, because myofilaments do not shorten during contraction. This option subtracts the whole 0.6 μm of sarcomere shortening from the A band. Misconception: believing the filaments (and therefore the A band) physically contract rather than slide.
option_analysis.C: Correct: the A band stays at the thick-filament length of 1.6 μm, and the H zone width = L − 2.0 = 2.0 − 2.0 = 0 μm because the thin-filament tips meet at the M line.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: 0.3 μm results from shrinking the H zone by only half of the sarcomere's shortening (0.6/2). The H zone actually shortens by the full 0.6 μm (0.3 μm of sliding at each end). Misconception: counting the sliding at only one Z line instead of both.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: keeps the H zone at its relaxed 0.6 μm value. The H zone must shrink as the thin filaments slide toward the centre. Misconception: treating the H zone as a fixed structure independent of sarcomere length.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Visual phototransduction: the dark current and the cGMP-gated cation channel
learning_objective: Reason about the mechanism of rod phototransduction to predict how locking the cGMP-gated channel open uncouples the light-activated cascade from the membrane response.
question: In vertebrate rod photoreceptors, cytoplasmic cGMP holds cation channels open in the dark, producing a steady inward 'dark current' that keeps the cell depolarised and releasing glutamate continuously. Absorption of light triggers a cascade (rhodopsin → transducin → phosphodiesterase) that lowers cGMP. A researcher applies a non-hydrolysable analogue of cGMP that keeps the cation channels open even when the light-activated phosphodiesterase is fully active. When a bright flash of light is delivered to a rod treated in this way, the rod membrane potential will most likely:

choices.A: hyperpolarise transiently and then depolarise, because guanylate cyclase resynthesises cGMP
choices.B: depolarise further, because light increases the cation permeability of the membrane
choices.C: lose its dark current entirely, because the analogue blocks the cation channel
choices.D: remain depolarised, because the cation channels stay open despite the fall in cytoplasmic cGMP
choices.E: hyperpolarise just as strongly as an untreated rod, because rhodopsin still bleaches normally

explanation: A rod's light response is a HYPERPOLARISATION caused by CLOSURE of the cGMP-gated cation channels: light lowers cGMP, cGMP unbinds, the channels shut, the inward dark current stops, the cell hyperpolarises, and glutamate release falls. The electrical response therefore depends entirely on the channels being able to close when cGMP drops. If a non-hydrolysable cGMP analogue holds the channels open regardless of the true cGMP level, then even a full light-driven fall in cGMP cannot shut them: the dark current persists, the rod stays depolarised, and no light signal is produced. The cascade upstream still runs, but it is now uncoupled from the membrane potential.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: guanylate cyclase does resynthesise cGMP during normal recovery, but here the channels never shut, so there is no initial hyperpolarisation to recover from. Misconception: importing the normal recovery phase into a situation where the response never occurs.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: light DECREASES cation entry (it closes channels); it does not increase permeability or depolarise the rod. Misconception: assuming a sensory stimulus must depolarise its receptor, as most receptors do.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: a non-hydrolysable cGMP analogue is an agonist that keeps the channel OPEN; it is not a channel blocker, so the dark current continues. Misconception: confusing a channel-opening analogue with an antagonist/blocker.
option_analysis.D: Correct: the hyperpolarising response needs the channels to close when cGMP falls; with them locked open, the dark current and depolarisation are maintained and the rod cannot signal light.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: rhodopsin bleaching and the biochemical cascade are only intermediate steps; the actual electrical response requires channel closure, which the analogue prevents. Misconception: equating activation of the photopigment directly with the membrane response.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Cochlear hair-cell mechanotransduction: K+ influx driven by the endocochlear potential
learning_objective: Combine chemical and electrical gradient information to deduce the direction of the transduction current in a cochlear hair cell and its effect on membrane potential.
question: The endolymph bathing the apical stereocilia of cochlear hair cells is unusual: it has a high K+ concentration (~150 mmol/L, similar to the hair-cell cytoplasm) and is held at about +80 mV (the endocochlear potential) relative to the hair-cell interior, which sits near −45 mV. When the stereocilia are deflected toward the tallest, the mechanically-gated cation channels at their tips open. What is the immediate ionic event across the apical membrane and its effect on the hair cell?

choices.A: Cl− flows into the hair cell and hyperpolarises it
choices.B: Na+ flows into the hair cell from the endolymph and depolarises it
choices.C: Ca2+ flows out of the hair cell and repolarises it
choices.D: K+ flows out of the hair cell and hyperpolarises it
choices.E: K+ flows into the hair cell and depolarises it

explanation: The chemical K+ gradient across the apical membrane is almost flat (about 150 mmol/L on both sides), so it barely drives K+ either way. The decisive factor is the electrical gradient: the endolymph is roughly +80 mV while the cell interior is about −45 mV, a difference of ~125 mV with the outside strongly positive. A positive-outside field drives the positive K+ ion inward. So when the transduction channels open, K+ flows INTO the hair cell and depolarises it; this depolarisation then opens basolateral voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and triggers neurotransmitter release. This is the rare case where opening a K+-permeable channel depolarises rather than hyperpolarises a cell, precisely because of the endocochlear potential.

option_analysis.A: Wrong: the transduction channels are cation-selective, and Cl− entry would in any case tend to hyperpolarise, not signal sound. Misconception: assuming an inhibitory anion current underlies transduction.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: it assumes any depolarising inward current must be Na+, but the endolymph is K+-rich and Na+-poor, so the charge carrier here is K+. Misconception: automatically equating depolarisation with Na+ influx.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: Ca2+ entry (not efflux) occurs later at the basolateral membrane to drive transmitter release; it is not the apical transduction current. Misconception: conflating the downstream synaptic Ca2+ signal with the initial mechanotransduction event.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: this applies the usual rule that K+ leaves cells through leak channels and hyperpolarises them, ignoring that the +80 mV endolymph reverses the driving force at the apical membrane. Misconception: 'K+ always flows out / K+ movement always hyperpolarises.'
option_analysis.E: Correct: with a negligible chemical gradient but a large positive endocochlear potential, the net electrochemical driving force pushes K+ into the cell through the open channels, depolarising it.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Coagulation cascade: localising a factor deficiency from PT and aPTT
learning_objective: Map the intrinsic, extrinsic and common coagulation pathways onto the PT and aPTT tests to localise a single-factor deficiency from a clinical pattern.
question: The prothrombin time (PT) tests the extrinsic and common pathways of coagulation, whereas the activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests the intrinsic and common pathways. A young man with a lifelong history of bleeding into his joints is found to have a normal PT but a markedly prolonged aPTT. A deficiency of which of the following clotting factors best explains this pattern?
explanation: A normal PT shows the extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the common pathway (factors X, V, II/prothrombin, fibrinogen) are intact. A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT therefore localises the defect to a factor unique to the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX or VIII). Recurrent bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) in a young male is the classic presentation of haemophilia A, a deficiency of factor VIII. Of the options given, only factor VIII is an intrinsic-limb factor that would leave the PT normal while prolonging the aPTT.

option_analysis.A: Correct: factor VIII is confined to the intrinsic pathway, so its deficiency prolongs the aPTT while leaving the PT normal, and joint bleeding in a young man fits haemophilia A.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: factor VII is the extrinsic-pathway factor, so its deficiency prolongs the PT and leaves the aPTT normal — the mirror image of the pattern described. Misconception: not tracking which pathway (and therefore which test) each factor belongs to.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: factor X is in the common pathway, so its deficiency prolongs BOTH the PT and the aPTT, not the aPTT alone. Misconception: forgetting that common-pathway factors affect both screening tests.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: fibrinogen is likewise a common-pathway factor, and its deficiency prolongs both PT and aPTT. Misconception: the same failure to recognise the shared common pathway.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: factor XIII cross-links fibrin AFTER the clot has already formed, so both PT and aPTT are normal even though the patient bleeds. Misconception: assuming every bleeding-factor deficiency must prolong a standard clotting time.

author: mioitalia_editorial

subject: biology
subtopic: Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation: arterial blood-gas interpretation
learning_objective: Integrate pH, PCO2 and bicarbonate to distinguish a primary metabolic disturbance with respiratory compensation from a primary respiratory disturbance, using pH direction to identify the primary process.
question: Normal arterial values are: pH 7.35–7.45, PCO2 about 40 mmHg, and HCO3− about 24 mmol/L. A patient who has had several days of severe watery diarrhoea (losing large amounts of bicarbonate) has arterial blood showing pH 7.30, HCO3− 15 mmol/L and PCO2 30 mmHg. Which of the following best describes the acid–base status?

choices.A: Metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation

explanation: First use the pH: 7.30 is below 7.35, so this is an acidaemia. Next find which measured variable has moved in the acidifying direction. A low HCO3− acidifies the blood (a metabolic cause), whereas a low PCO2 alkalinises it (it cannot be the cause of an acidosis). Therefore the primary disturbance is a metabolic acidosis — consistent with the loss of bicarbonate in the diarrhoea. The low PCO2 is not a primary problem but the respiratory compensation: the patient hyperventilates to blow off CO2 and pull the pH back toward normal. Because the pH is still below the normal range, the compensation is only partial. The key discriminator is that respiratory alkalosis would also show a low PCO2 but would RAISE the pH above 7.45; here the pH is low, proving the low PCO2 is compensatory, not primary.

option_analysis.A: Correct: low pH with low HCO3− is a primary metabolic acidosis (bicarbonate loss from diarrhoea), and the low PCO2 is compensatory hyperventilation; the pH remaining below 7.35 shows the compensation is only partial.
option_analysis.B: Wrong: the low PCO2 is consistent with respiratory alkalosis, but a primary respiratory alkalosis would raise the pH above normal. The low pH shows the low PCO2 is compensation, not the primary event. Misconception: reading PCO2 first and mistaking the compensatory change for the primary disorder — the classic trap.
option_analysis.C: Wrong: an alkalosis requires pH above 7.45 and, if metabolic, a HIGH HCO3−; this patient has a low pH and low HCO3−. Misconception: ignoring the pH direction when naming the disorder.
option_analysis.D: Wrong: the PCO2 is low, not high, so there is no respiratory acidosis at all, and the disturbance is clearly compensated (PCO2 has shifted). Misconception: confusing which variable marks a respiratory disorder.
option_analysis.E: Wrong: respiratory acidosis requires a HIGH PCO2 (CO2 retention) with a compensatory HIGH HCO3−; here both are low. Misconception: labelling any acidosis 'respiratory' without checking that PCO2 is actually raised.

author: mioitalia_editorial
